## **Modeling Breeding Bird Survey with bbsBayes2: status, trends, and causal modeling of drivers of trends**

## Monday, 8 October, 2026, 14:00-16:30 EDT

## 

**Lead**:

Adam C. Smith (Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment and Climate Change Canada) [adam.smith\@ec.gc.ca](mailto:adam.smith@ec.gc.ca) Adam C. Smith on

### About the workshop

[bbsBayes2](https://bbsbayes.github.io/bbsBayes2) is an R-package that allows for easy access to the North American Breeding Bird Survey data and for fitting a selection of hierarchical Bayesian models that estimate status and trends and can be modified to estimate the influence of spatial and temporal predictors on trends and abundance (e.g., [Mckellar et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1675/063.048.0203) and [Smith et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1093/ornithapp/duad056)). The package provides efficient, fully-Bayesian parameter estimation using Stan, spatially explicit models well suited to exploring spatial patterns in trends, and options to customize models to include covariates of trends and abundance. The package also allows for a streamlined Bayesian workflow that facilitates convergence diagnostics, prior and posterior predictions, visualization of model predictions, as well as cross-validation and model comparisons.

During this workshop you will follow along with live coding to get hands-on experience manipulating and visualizing output from a range of models and species. We will demonstrate the package’s functions, including those that allow you to:

1.  Prepare the data for modeling a given species and fit a model that estimates trends for any time period (1970-2019, 2005-2015, 1980-2000, etc.)
2.  Generate heat maps of population trends and graph population trajectories.
3.  Choose from a suite of built-in hierarchical Bayesian models and access tools to help with cross-validation and model comparison.
4.  Estimate trends for customized regions (e.g., all of the eastern Boreal, Great Plains versus eastern populations of grassland birds).
5.  Build and fit customized models: the workshop allows some time to explore customizing the base-models with examples of models that estimate regional climate-effects on population trends, local landcover effects on mean abundance, landcover change effects on trends, etc.

## To do before the workshop

To make the workshop as efficient as possible, please ensure that you have completed the following steps prior to the workshop.

#### 1. Fill in the [pre-workshop survey](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeEFM_nShyszyTTcwZVge8GviwxBkSJz_muyL6heIhLW2Z_Hg/viewform?usp=publish-editor)

#### 2. Install software and download BBS data

Run the installation steps at the beginning of the [Getting Started Vignette](https://bbsbayes.github.io/bbsBayes2/) including:

1.  Install the latest release of bbsBayes2 (please update if you have previously installed it)

2.  [Install cmdstanr](https://bbsbayes.github.io/bbsBayes2/articles/bbsBayes2.html#install-cmdstanr) and confirm that your setup is correct.

3.  Download the BBS data `bbsBayes2::fetch_bbs_data()`.

**If you are having problems with these installations, you're welcome to email [me](mailto:adam.smith@ec.gc.ca). I will do my best to help.**

#### 2. Download fitted model files

In addition, please download these zip files (from a Google Drive, links below) that include stored model output and an alternate stratification map that we'll use during the workshop. These additional files will allow us to try out the summary functions (trends, trajectories, trend maps, etc.), without having to run the models yourself (BBS models can require hours or longer to finish sampling). Once downloaded, unzip them to a directory called *`output`* within the working directory where you expect to do your coding during the workshop.

## Workshop plan

We will start by demonstrating some of the [basic workflow](https://bbsbayes.github.io/bbsBayes2/articles/bbsBayes2.html#workflow-overview) for using the package, largely using examples from the package vignettes. Then I'll demonstrate some ways to modify the base models to include covariates on the species' abundance or changes in abundance.
